field:comments — Findings

The findings, one object per finding. May be empty only when verdict is approve;
a request_changes or comment verdict with no comments is not a review with a
quality problem, it is a review that failed to say anything. Each comment
carries a reviewer-authored id, a priority, a category, a body, a list of
anchors and a list of suggestions. Four occurrences of the same problem are one
comment with four anchors, not four comments. More than 25 comments raises
comment-flood.
related: id, priority, anchors, suggestions

field:comments.anchors — Where the finding applies

Zero or more locations the finding applies to, each a repository-relative path
with an optional line or line span, read at the document ref. A list, because
one finding can occur at four call sites — that is one comment with four
anchors, not four comments. Architectural findings with no single location may
carry none, but the array is required and empty is the way to say so. Anchors
describe where the problem is; where a fix lands and how far it reaches is the
suggestion's scope, and the two are frequently different. Anchors are checked
against the repository: a path or line that does not exist at the document ref
is an error, not an advisory.
related: file, line, ref, scope

field:comments.anchors.end_line — Span end

1-indexed inclusive last line of the span. Requires line and must be greater
than or equal to it; end_line without line, or before it, is a structural error
(anchor-range-ordered). Omit for a single-line anchor rather than repeating
line. Note the underscore: end-line is rejected, because a permissive schema
would drop the misspelling silently and leave a review claiming a one-line span
the reviewer never meant.

example: 94
related: line, anchor-range-ordered

field:comments.anchors.file — File path

A repository-relative POSIX path: no leading slash, no .. segment, no
backslashes. internal/fetch/client.go, never
/home/me/repo/internal/fetch/client.go and never ../other/client.go. The path is
checked against the repository at the document ref, so a file that does not
exist there is an error naming the ref it was looked up in.

example: "internal/fetch/client.go"
related: line, ref, anchor-path-safe

field:comments.anchors.line — Line number

1-indexed line the comment applies to. Omit for a file-level comment — an
anchor with only a file is valid and is the right shape for "this file needs a
test". The number is verified against the file at the document ref, so it must
be a line that exists there; a plausible-looking line number is exactly the
error this format exists to catch. A line in a document with no ref raises
ref-missing, because nobody can ever check it.

example: 88
related: end_line, file, ref

field:comments.body — Finding and rationale

The finding and why it matters, 20-4000 characters. State what is wrong, then
the consequence — "passes context.Background(), so a cancelled request keeps
retrying for the full backoff schedule" is actionable where "context handling is
wrong" is not. Under 60 characters raises body-thin; low-signal text ("lgtm",
"looks good", "see above", "consider refactoring" with nothing following) raises
vacuous-body. Two comments with identical bodies raise duplicate-body. Where the
fix goes belongs in a suggestion, not here.

example: "The retry loop calls c.do(context.Background(), req) rather than passing the caller's ctx, so a cancelled request keeps retrying."
related: comments.code, suggestions, body-thin

field:comments.category — Category

What kind of finding this is. correctness — wrong behaviour, logic errors,
unhandled cases. security — vulnerabilities, unsafe handling of untrusted
input or secrets. performance — avoidable cost in time, memory or I/O.
maintainability — structure, naming, duplication, complexity. testing —
missing, weak or misleading tests. documentation — missing or incorrect
comments, docs or godoc. style — formatting and convention adherence. The
first three can carry any priority; the last four conventionally stay below the
blocking band, and one filed at 9-10 raises priority-category-convention rather
than being rejected.

example: "correctness"
related: priority, priority-category-convention

field:comments.code — Code excerpt

An optional illustrative excerpt. On a comment it shows the problematic code as
it stands; on a suggestion it shows that code as the suggestion would leave it.
Read together they show the change without anyone opening a file, and one before
can be quoted against several afters. Both are deliberately soft: no line
numbers, no fences, matched against nothing, verified by nothing, and carrying
none of an anchor's constraints. Truncate freely, elide the middle, trim context
to whatever makes the point. Nothing downstream may treat it as authoritative,
and it must never be applied as a patch — a soft excerpt that gets applied is
a patch that silently corrupts a file. Often absent: a missing test has no code
to quote.

example: "resp, err := c.do(context.Background(), req)"
related: anchors, suggestions

field:comments.id — Comment identifier

A reviewer-authored identifier: a short kebab-case slug naming the kind of
finding, then a numeric suffix, e.g. missing-context-2. Pattern
^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*-[1-9][0-9]*$; keep the slug under 48 characters and
five words. The slug groups: four findings of the same kind share it, so a
consumer collapses them into one theme without reading four bodies. The suffix
addresses one finding, so an orchestrator can say "resolve missing-context-2".
There is no controlled vocabulary — naming the finding is part of the job, and
describe-2 or issue-1 throws the grouping away. Ids are unique within a
document, and suffixes within a slug run contiguously from 1.

example: "missing-context-2"
related: id-unique, id-grouping

field:comments.priority — Priority

Integer 1-10, higher is more urgent. 9-10 must fix before merge: the change is
wrong or unsafe as it stands. 7-8 should fix before merge: a real defect or
design problem, not a preference. 4-6 worth fixing, does not block. 1-3 optional
polish the author may decline without justification. Use the range, not the
endpoints — four or more comments at one value raises priority-flat, the
signal that the scale went unused. A comment at 7 or above with no suggestions
raises suggestion-absent. testing, maintainability, documentation and style
filed at 9-10 raise priority-category-convention; there is no floor, and a
security finding at 2 is fine.

example: 9
related: category, suggestions, priority-flat

field:comments.suggestions — Proposed fixes

Zero or more competing ways to address the finding, each with its effort, its
blast radius, its pros and its cons. A list because the useful case is offering
a choice: "patch this call site" and "make the mistake unexpressible at the type
level" answer the same finding at different cost and different risk, and a
reviewer presenting one has quietly made the orchestrator's decision for it.
Required, and may be empty — but a comment at priority 7 or above with no
suggestions raises suggestion-absent, and a comment whose only suggestion is
module or project scope raises broad-scope-alone.
related: effort, scope, pros, cons

field:comments.suggestions.code — Resulting code

An optional illustrative excerpt of the code as this suggestion would leave it
— the after to the comment's before. It lives on the suggestion rather than
the comment because competing suggestions produce different code: a line-scope
option rewrites the call site where a module-scope option answering the same
finding changes the exported signature. One before, several afters, and a
consumer choosing between them can see the difference without opening a file.
Soft, exactly like the comment's excerpt: no line numbers, no fences, matched
against nothing, verified by nothing. Truncate and elide freely. It is not a
patch and must never be applied as one.

example: "resp, err := c.do(ctx, req)"
related: comments.code, comments.suggestions.summary

field:comments.suggestions.cons — Downsides

What this option costs or risks, one string per point. Required; may be empty,
but an empty list raises suggestion-no-cons, and an empty list on a module or
project suggestion also raises broad-scope-no-cons. A suggestion with no stated
downside is either trivially correct or under-examined, and the difference
matters to whoever has to choose. If the fix really is free, an empty list plus
the advisory is the honest record; reaching module or project scope is never
free.

example: ["Breaks the exported signature; every caller must be updated"]
related: pros, broad-scope-no-cons

field:comments.suggestions.effort — Level of effort

How much work the suggestion is, as one of four buckets. trivial — a line or
two, no design decision, no new tests. small — contained in one function or
file, under an hour. medium — spans several files or needs a design choice,
under a day. large — structural change, migration, or new subsystem. An
ordinal enum rather than a number because effort estimates from a model are not
precise enough to justify a 1-10 scale. Effort is independent of scope, and
keeping them apart is the point: one shared constant is trivial effort with
project blast radius.

example: "trivial"
related: scope, suggestions

field:comments.suggestions.pros — Upsides

Why this option is worth taking, one string per point. Required; may be empty,
but an empty list raises suggestion-no-pros. Say what this option buys that the
alternatives do not — "cancellation propagates immediately", "makes the
deadline impossible to drop rather than fixing one site" — since the value of
listing several suggestions is that a consumer can tell them apart.

example: ["Cancellation and deadlines propagate immediately"]
related: cons, suggestions

field:comments.suggestions.scope — Blast radius

How far applying this suggestion reaches — what else has to be re-read,
re-tested or re-approved. line: a line or a few adjacent lines, nothing beyond
them. block: one function, method or type body, callers unaffected. file:
structure within one file, the package's exported surface unchanged. module:
several files, or a package's exported surface, so other packages must adapt.
project: architecture, conventions, tooling or a public API; repository-wide. A
property of the fix, not of the finding — the same finding can be answered at
several radii, which is why scope sits here and not on the comment. A lone
module or project suggestion raises broad-scope-alone.

example: "line"
related: effort, broad-scope-alone

field:comments.suggestions.summary — Suggestion summary

What to do, in one sentence, 10-500 characters. Name the change and where it
goes — "pass the caller's context straight through to c.do" — rather than
restating the finding. This is the field an orchestrator reads when choosing
between competing suggestions, so two suggestions on one comment should be
distinguishable from their summaries alone. The optional code field shows the
result; the summary says what the move is.

example: "Pass the caller's context straight through to c.do"
related: effort, scope, comments.suggestions.code

field:ref — Reviewed commit

The commit the review was performed against: a full 40-character lowercase SHA,
and nothing else. Not a branch, not a tag, not an abbreviation — a branch
names a moving target, so an anchor recorded against main means whatever main
points at when someone looks, which reads as precision while being unverifiable.
git rev-parse HEAD produces the correct value. Set it once at the root: it is
the commit every anchor in the document is read at. There is deliberately no
per-anchor ref — a review is of one change at one revision, and a comment that
needs to talk about a second revision says so in its body. Optional, because not
every review is of a git repository — but an anchor carrying a line number in
a document with no ref raises ref-missing, since that line number can never be
checked by anyone.

example: "4f2c1a9e8b3d7c5a1f0e2d4b6a8c9e1f3a5b7c9d"
related: anchors, line, ref-format

field:summary — Overall assessment

One to three sentences assessing the change as a whole, 30-1500 characters.
Consumers read it without opening the comments, so state what is actually wrong
and what holds up — restating the verdict ("changes requested") wastes the
field. Under 60 characters on a review with three or more comments raises
summary-thin. A suggestion's one-line summary is a different field:
comments.suggestions.summary.

example: "The retry loop is sound, but the context deadline is not propagated to the downstream call, so a cancelled request keeps retrying."
related: verdict, comments

field:verdict — Overall disposition

The review's overall disposition. approve — the change should land as it
stands. request_changes — something has to change first. comment —
observations, with no gate either way. Nothing relates the verdict to comment
priorities: approve while filing a priority-10 note, or request changes over a
single 4, if that is your judgement. Reconciling verdict and priorities is the
reviewer's job and no check second-guesses it. A request_changes or comment
verdict must carry at least one comment; approve may carry none, and that is the
only case where an empty comments array validates.

example: "request_changes"
related: comments, priority

field:version — Format version

Format version. Always the string "1" — a string, not a number. Any other
value is rejected outright. The field is not a compatibility scheme; it exists
so a future consumer can recognise a format it does not understand and say so.

example: "1"
related: verdict, comments

check:document-unparseable — Unparseable document

Fires when the input never became a document: malformed JSON, a top-level value
that is not an object, or a second value after the first. It is the one failure
that stops the run, because there is nothing left to check — every other check
reports against a document, and here there is none.

No other diagnostic accompanies it. Do not read that quiet as approval of the
rest: nothing else ran.

The usual causes are prose wrapped around the JSON, a fenced code block left in,
and two documents concatenated into one stream. The message carries the
decoder's own complaint, which names the byte offset:

  refinery validate review.json
  invalid character 'h' looking for beginning of value

This is a document to repair rather than a command line to fix, so it exits 1
like any other unusable document.
related: schema, tiers, verdict

check:schema — Schema conformance

Fires when the document does not conform to the embedded JSON Schema: a missing
required field, a value of the wrong type, an out-of-range priority, an enum
value that is not in the enum, or a field name the format does not define. Each
failure is reported with a JSON Pointer into your document, so the third column
tells you exactly where to look.

Unknown fields are rejected on purpose: the failure this format exists to catch
is the mistake that reads as correct, and a misspelled key is exactly that.
Write "end-line" and a permissive schema drops it silently, leaving a review
that validates clean while claiming a span you never meant. When the unknown
name is close to a real one the diagnostic says so:

  unknown field "end-line" — did you mean "end_line"?

Open the lens for the field the diagnostic names — for "12 is greater than the
maximum of 10" that is the priority scale, not JSON Schema.
related: version, comments, priority

check:id-unique — Duplicate comment id

Fires when two comments carry the same id. Ids are how every consumer refers to
a finding — a diagnostic, an orchestrator saying "resolve missing-context-2",
a human reading a digest — so a duplicate makes one of the two findings
unaddressable, and nothing downstream can tell which one was meant.

Fix it by renumbering rather than renaming. The slug is the grouping mechanism,
so two findings of the same kind belong on the same slug and differ only in
suffix; inventing a second slug to dodge the collision throws away the grouping
that made the ids worth having.

  before: "missing-context-1", "missing-context-1"
  after:  "missing-context-1", "missing-context-2"
related: id, id-grouping

check:anchor-range-ordered — Anchor span out of order

Fires when an anchor carries end_line without line, or an end_line before its
line. A span that runs backwards names no lines at all, and an end_line with no
start has no anchor point, so neither can be resolved by anyone reading the
review later.

Drop end_line for a single-line anchor rather than repeating line; the span is
inclusive, so line 88 with end_line 94 is seven lines.

  before: { "file": "internal/fetch/client.go", "line": 94, "end_line": 88 }
  after:  { "file": "internal/fetch/client.go", "line": 88, "end_line": 94 }
related: line, end_line, anchors

check:anchor-path-safe — Unsafe anchor path

Fires when an anchor's file is not a plain repository-relative POSIX path: a
leading slash, a ".." segment, or a backslash anywhere. An absolute path names a
location on the reviewing machine, which nobody else has; a ".." segment names a
file outside the repository the ref belongs to, so no commit can confirm it; a
backslash is a Windows path that will not resolve in git.

Write the path exactly as git reports it — git ls-files output is always the
right shape.

  before: "/home/me/repo/internal/fetch/client.go", "../other/client.go"
  after:  "internal/fetch/client.go"
related: file, anchors

check:ref-format — Malformed ref

Fires when the document ref is not 40 lowercase hex characters. There is one
ref, at the root, and every anchor is read at it. Branches and tags are rejected
because they name a moving target: an anchor recorded against "main" means
whatever main points at when someone looks, which is not what was reviewed, and
nothing in the document records the difference. Abbreviations are rejected
because they are unambiguous only until the repository grows.

This is checkable without a repository, so it fires even when verification is
skipped. git rev-parse HEAD produces the correct value, and a reviewing agent is
holding a checkout already.

  before: "main", "4f2c1a9"
  after:  "4f2c1a9e8b3d7c5a1f0e2d4b6a8c9e1f3a5b7c9d"
related: ref, ref-unknown, ref-missing

check:verification-required — Verification required but unavailable

Fires only under --require-verification, and says one thing: nobody confirmed
these anchors. A repository that did not answer, a commit this checkout does not
have, a file git could not read — different causes, same answer.

Without the flag that is reported and the run passes, because a document is not
wrong for being checked somewhere that could not check it. The flag is for the
caller who cannot accept that: a merge gate whose whole purpose is confirming
the line numbers are real, where a review nobody verified is worth no more than
no review.

The status line carries the cause: "not a git repository" means cd, an
unavailable source means the machine rather than the review, and a skipped
anchor names its file. --warn-only demotes this like any other verification
check — coherent to ask for, worth noticing that you did.
related: ref-unknown, anchor-file-missing, tiers

check:ref-unknown — Unresolvable ref

Fires when the document ref names no commit in the repository the tool was run
in. Every anchor is read at that ref, so the whole review becomes a set of
claims nobody can check — which is why it is reported once for the document
rather than once per anchor.

There are two ordinary causes. Either you are in the wrong repository, in which
case the SHA in the diagnostic will look foreign and the fix is to cd; or the
commit is genuinely absent — a shallow clone, or a branch deleted and garbage
collected since the review was written. That second case is what --warn-only is
for: it demotes the verification checks to advisories so a legitimate gap does
not fail the run.

If the ref is wrong rather than absent, take it from the checkout the review was
performed against: git rev-parse HEAD. Fetching the commit is the other fix;
refinery never touches the network itself.
related: ref, ref-format, anchor-file-missing

check:anchor-file-missing — Anchored file missing

Fires when an anchor's path does not exist at the document ref, or names a
directory rather than a file. The diagnostic names the ref it looked in, so the
claim can be checked by hand:

  git ls-tree -r --name-only 4f2c1a9 | grep client

The usual causes are a path invented from memory, a path relative to a
subdirectory rather than the repository root, and a file that exists in the
working tree but not at the reviewed commit. Anchors are repository-relative
from the root, always — internal/fetch/client.go, never fetch/client.go
because that is where you happened to be standing.

An anchor pointing at nothing makes its comment unactionable, which is why this
is an error rather than an advisory. A comment with no location at all is
legitimate: file it with an empty anchors list.
related: file, anchors, ref-unknown

check:anchor-line-out-of-range — Anchored line out of range

Fires when an anchor's line or end_line is past the end of the file at the
document ref. The diagnostic names the file's real length and the ref, because
"line 88 is out of range" invites an argument and "line 88 is out of range in a
61-line file at 4f2c1a9" ends it.

This is the check that catches the failure this format exists for: a
hallucinated line number is well-formed, plausibly numbered, and wrong, and no
amount of care elsewhere in the review makes it inspectable. Confirm the span
before filing it:

  git show 4f2c1a9:internal/fetch/client.go | sed -n '88,94p'

refinery only confirms the line exists. Whether it is the right line is your job
— that is why a file-level anchor, with no line at all, is a legitimate answer
when you are not certain.
related: line, end_line, anchors

check:id-grouping — Non-contiguous id suffixes

Fires when the suffixes on a slug do not run 1, 2, 3 — a gap (foo-1, foo-3), a
start above 1, or a slug used once as foo-2. Nothing breaks, but the gap reads
as a missing finding: a consumer collapsing a slug into one theme cannot tell
whether foo-2 was dropped on purpose or lost in an edit.

The slug is the grouping mechanism and the suffix is the address, so number
within a slug from 1 and stay contiguous. Do not renumber to dodge a collision
between different kinds of finding — give those different slugs.

  before: "missing-context-1", "missing-context-3"
  after:  "missing-context-1", "missing-context-2"
related: id, id-unique

check:ref-missing — Line number with no ref

Fires when an anchor carries a line number and the document supplies no ref. A
line number without a commit is a claim about a moment nobody recorded: the line
it meant is somewhere else the instant anything moves, and no reader — a
person, a later agent, a CI job — can ever check it.

The fix is one field at the document root, inherited by every anchor:

  "ref": "4f2c1a9e8b3d7c5a1f0e2d4b6a8c9e1f3a5b7c9d"

git rev-parse HEAD produces it, and you are holding a checkout already. It is an
advisory rather than an error because not every review is of a git repository;
if yours is not, drop the line numbers and anchor at file level instead of
recording numbers nobody can resolve.
related: ref, line, ref-format

check:body-thin — Thin comment body

Fires when a body is under 60 characters once whitespace is normalized. It meets
the schema minimum but is unlikely to carry a rationale, and a finding without
one is a preference the author can dismiss without cost.

A body should say what is wrong and what follows from it. The consequence is the
part that survives the trip to whoever fixes it.

  before: "Context handling is wrong here."
  after:  "The retry loop passes context.Background() rather than the caller's
           ctx, so a cancelled request keeps retrying for the full backoff
           schedule, holding the connection past the caller's deadline."

Length is a proxy, not the point: a genuinely one-line finding that names the
symptom and the consequence will clear 60 characters on its own.
related: body, vacuous-body

check:vacuous-body — Vacuous comment body

Fires when a body, normalized and lowercased, is nothing but a low-signal
phrase: "lgtm", "looks good", "no issues", "see above", "consider refactoring"
with nothing following. These pass the schema's length floor while transferring
no information, and they are the exact failure mode this format exists to catch
— a hollow review that is indistinguishable from a real one downstream.

"See above" is worth calling out separately: a comment is addressed by id and
read in isolation, so a body that refers to another comment by position is
unreadable to the consumer that received only this one. Name the id, or repeat
the finding.

  before: "Consider refactoring."
  after:  "parseHeader and parseTrailer differ only in the delimiter; folding
           them into one function keeps the two parsers from drifting."
related: body, body-thin

check:suggestion-absent — High-priority finding with no suggestion

Fires when a comment at priority 7 or above carries no suggestions. At that
priority you are saying the change should not merge as it stands, so the
orchestrator has to act — and with no suggestion it has to derive the fix from
your prose, which is the work you were asked to do.

One suggestion is enough when there is one move. Two are better when the finding
can be answered at different blast radii: patch the call site, or change the
type so the mistake stops being expressible.

  "suggestions": [{ "summary": "Pass the caller's ctx through to c.do",
    "effort": "trivial", "scope": "line", "pros": ["Deadlines propagate"],
    "cons": ["Callers relying on the old behaviour see a change"] }]

If you cannot propose anything, the priority is usually too high: lower it and
say what you are unsure about.
related: suggestions, priority

check:suggestion-no-cons — Suggestion with no stated downside

Fires when a suggestion's cons list is empty. A fix with no stated downside is
either trivially correct or under-examined, and the consumer choosing between
your suggestions cannot tell which — that difference is most of the value of
offering a choice at all.

State the cost even when it is small: a behaviour change some caller may rely
on, a test that has to be rewritten, a signature other packages import.

  "cons": ["Callers relying on retries outliving the request context see a
            behaviour change"]

If the fix really is free, say so in a pro ("no caller-visible change") and
carry the advisory. It is a note that the tradeoff was examined and found empty,
not a finding that you were wrong.
related: cons, pros, broad-scope-no-cons

check:suggestion-no-pros — Suggestion with no stated upside

Fires when a suggestion's pros list is empty. With one suggestion the omission
is mild; with two it is the whole problem, because a consumer choosing between
them has only the summaries to go on and no statement of what each option buys.

Say what this option gets that the alternatives do not — and say it in terms
of consequences, not restatement of the summary.

  before: "pros": []
  after:  "pros": ["Cancellation propagates immediately",
                   "Nothing outside the loop body has to be re-read"]

An empty list is legal, and sometimes honest for a fix whose only merit is that
it is correct. Filling it in costs one line and makes the comparison possible.
related: pros, cons

check:broad-scope-alone — Wide fix offered with no alternative

Fires when a comment's single suggestion has scope module or project. A wide
blast radius offered with no narrower alternative gives the orchestrator no
choice exactly where the choice costs most: it can take a change that reaches
other packages or the whole repository, or it can take nothing.

Offer the narrow option too, even if you prefer the wide one. Scope sits on the
suggestion precisely because one finding can be answered at several radii.

  1. "Pass the caller's context through at this call site"  — scope: line
  2. "Take a context on the exported Fetch method"          — scope: module

The advisory does not say the wide fix is wrong. It says the consumer should be
allowed to defer it, and that deferring is only possible if you named something
smaller.
related: scope, suggestions, broad-scope-no-cons

check:broad-scope-no-cons — Wide fix with no stated cost

Fires when a suggestion at scope module or project has an empty cons list.
Reaching that far always costs something — other packages adapt, an exported
signature breaks, a convention has to be applied everywhere it was not — and a
wide change presented as free is the one a consumer is most likely to apply
without checking.

Name what has to be re-read, re-tested or re-approved:

  "scope": "module",
  "cons": ["Breaks the exported signature; every caller of Fetch is updated",
           "Larger blast radius than the defect strictly requires"]

This fires alongside suggestion-no-cons, which is deliberate: the empty list is
worth one note on its own and another when the fix is this wide.
related: scope, cons, broad-scope-alone

check:summary-thin — Thin review summary

Fires when the document summary is under 60 characters and the review carries
three or more comments. The summary is what a consumer reads when it will not
read twelve comments, so on a review with real findings it has to carry the
shape of them — not restate the verdict, which is already a field.

  before: "Changes requested."
  after:  "The retry loop is sound, but the context deadline is not propagated
           to the downstream call, so a cancelled request keeps retrying until
           the attempt budget is exhausted."

One to three sentences is the target. Say what holds up as well as what does
not: a summary that only lists problems reads as a rejection even when the
verdict is comment.
related: field:summary, verdict

check:priority-category-convention — Category above the blocking band

Fires when a testing, maintainability, documentation or style comment is filed
at priority 9 or 10 — the band that says the change must not merge as it
stands. Those four categories conventionally sit below it: a formatting
complaint is not a reason to stop a change, however strongly you feel about it.

The format encodes no ceiling per category; any such table would invent
precision nobody has. This is a note that a convention was crossed, not a
finding that you were wrong — undocumented behaviour in a public API genuinely
can be worth blocking on, and a reviewer who means it should say so in the body
and carry the advisory.

  before: category "documentation", priority 9, "godoc missing on Fetch"
  after:  priority 5 — or keep 9 and justify it in the body

There is no floor: a security finding at priority 2 is fine.
related: priority, category

check:priority-flat — Flat priority distribution

Fires when a review carries four or more comments and every one of them has the
same priority. A subset sharing a priority is ordinary and says nothing; it is
the absence of any spread across the whole review that suggests the scale was
not used: the field exists so a consumer can sort, threshold and merge across
reviewers, and a review where everything is a 7 gives it nothing to sort by.

Spread the findings across the bands you actually mean. 9-10 must fix before
merge. 7-8 should fix, a real defect. 4-6 worth fixing, does not block. 1-3
optional polish the author may decline.

  before: 7, 7, 7, 7
  after:  9, 7, 5, 2

This is an aggregate check: it runs only when every comment has a usable
priority, because a confident claim computed over the subset that happened to
parse is worse than no claim. If one priority is ill-typed you will see this
reported as skipped rather than answered.
related: priority, category

check:duplicate-anchor — Two comments on one span

Fires when two comments anchor the identical span — same file, line and
end_line. Usually it is one finding filed twice, which costs the consumer two
reads to discover they are the same thing.

If they really are two findings about one span, they should have different
anchors or be one comment carrying two suggestions. If it is one finding with
several fixes, that is exactly what the suggestions list is for.

  before: two comments, both anchored at client.go:88-94
  after:  one comment at client.go:88-94 with two suggestions

Two anchors on the same file at different lines are not duplicates, and neither
is the same finding filed once with several anchors — that is what the anchors
list is for.
related: anchors, suggestions, duplicate-body

check:duplicate-body — Repeated comment body

Fires when two comments carry the same body once whitespace is normalized. The
same text filed twice is either a copy-paste that lost its second finding, or
one finding split across two ids for no reason a consumer can see.

If it is genuinely the same problem in several places, that is one comment with
several anchors — the anchors list exists for exactly this, and filing it once
keeps the finding and its suggestions together:

  before: two comments, identical bodies, one anchor each
  after:  one comment, two anchors

If the findings differ, say how in each body. A consumer reading them side by
side has nothing else to go on.
related: body, anchors, duplicate-anchor

check:comment-flood — Too many comments

Fires when a review carries more than 25 comments. Feedback at that volume is
not actionable: nobody triages it in one pass, and the findings that matter are
buried among the ones that do not.

Two things usually fix it. Collapse repetition — the same unchecked error at
nine call sites is one comment with nine anchors, not nine comments. And drop
the 1-3 band entirely on a large change: optional polish is what a consumer
discards first anyway, and filing it costs the same attention as a defect.

If more than 25 distinct blocking findings really are present, the honest report
is usually a summary saying the change needs restructuring, with the strongest
handful anchored.

This is an aggregate check and runs only when every element of comments is an
object; otherwise it is reported as skipped.
related: comments, duplicate-body

topic:effort-vs-scope — Effort and blast radius

Every suggestion carries two independent ordinals, and keeping them apart is the
point.

effort is how much work: trivial, small, medium, large. scope is blast radius,
what else has to be re-read or re-tested: line, block, file, module, project.

They come apart constantly: one shared constant is trivial effort with project
blast radius, a gnarly parser internal large effort with block radius. An
orchestrator triaging needs both:

                narrow radius     wide radius
  low effort    apply it          cheap but far-reaching; check first
  high effort   schedule it       escalate; this is its own change

scope sits on the suggestion because one finding can be answered at several
radii: patch this call site, or change the type so the mistake stops being
expressible. The choice belongs to the caller, which is why a lone module or
project suggestion raises broad-scope-alone.
related: effort, scope, suggestions, broad-scope-alone

topic:ids — Comment ids and grouping

Every comment carries a reviewer-authored id: a kebab-case slug naming the kind
of finding, then a numeric suffix — missing-context-2, unchecked-error-1.

The slug groups and the suffix addresses. Four findings of the same kind share a
slug, so a consumer collapses missing-context-1 through -4 into one theme
without reading four bodies; the suffix means an orchestrator can say "resolve
missing-context-2" and both sides know which finding is meant.

There is no controlled vocabulary. Naming the finding is part of reviewing:
unchecked-error groups with other unchecked errors, where client-go-1 and
issue-1 group with nothing.

Ids are unique within a document — a duplicate makes one finding
unaddressable, which is a structural error. Suffixes within a slug run
contiguously from 1; a gap raises id-grouping, because a consumer cannot tell a
deliberate gap from a lost finding.
related: id, id-unique, id-grouping

topic:tiers — Check tiers and exit codes

Checks come in three tiers answering different questions.

Structural checks ask "is this a document?" — schema conformance, unique ids,
safe paths, well-formed refs. Always run, always hard.

Verification checks ask "is this about anything real?" — does this path exist
at this ref, does the file have this many lines. Errors when a repository
answers. --warn-only demotes them for one lacking the reviewed commit;
--require-verification makes a skip an error.

Advisory checks ask "is this a good review?" — a thin body, a suggestion with
no stated cost, every comment at priority 9. Always run, never fatal. --strict
promotes them, --disable silences named ones.

Exit 0 is valid, exit 1 means revise the review, exit 2 means fix the
invocation. Only document-unparseable gates the rest; otherwise one run reports
everything findable, and checks that cannot run are listed as skipped, not
passed.
related: schema, ref-unknown, priority-flat

topic:verification — Anchors as checkable claims

An anchor says: this path, at this commit, has this line. That is a factual
claim, and the one an agent gets wrong most confidently: a hallucinated line
number is well-formed, plausibly numbered, and wrong.

So the document carries a ref: a full 40-character commit SHA, never a branch. A
branch names a moving target — an anchor recorded against main means whatever
main points at when someone looks, stale without ever changing.

validate checks those claims against the repository it is run in, by default and
with no flag, by object lookup — a commit that is not checked out still
resolves. With no repository the tier is skipped, and reported as skipped.

refinery confirms the anchor points somewhere; whether it points at the right
line is the reviewer's job. What the SHA buys is that anyone can check:

  git show 4f2c1a9:internal/fetch/client.go | sed -n '88,94p'
related: anchors, file, line, ref, anchor-file-missing
